caption: Macular hole closure with passive aspiration and air-fluid exchange.
transcript: By passively aspirating the fluid under the PFCL, we can see that the macular hole appears to close. While intraoperative OCT wasn't used in this case, it was used in the paper by Sabatino to confirm macular hole closure. You can see here the before and after intraoperative photos demonstrating closure of the macular hole. Lastly, an air-fluid exchange is performed to completely remove the PFCL bubble, and the case is complete. So here's some take-home points. This is a very interesting and novel approach to macular hole closure that obviates the need for an ILM flap. Now this case was a medium-sized macular hole, and so ILM flaps likely would not have been necessary to achieve successful closure, but in the series published by Sabatino and colleagues, the macular holes ranged in size from 682 to 918 microns. This may also be a useful technique in macular hole re-operation where ILM peeling has already been performed, thereby avoiding the need for an ILM free flap or other techniques to close the macular hole. When performing this technique, it's important only to use passive aspiration with a fluted soft tip cannula to remove any residual fluid in the macular hole and to avoid contact with the RPE and retina that may result in iatrogenic damage. A high magnification contact lens may be helpful here to ensure proper positioning of the soft tip over the macular hole. The series published by Sabatino only included five macular holes, so more data is needed on the long-term success and visual outcomes of this technique. Additionally, all cases in that series were treated with an iso-expand cell concentration of gas, and the question remains whether air fill alone may have been adequate to achieve closure.
